CWE-183.name: Permissive List of Allowed Inputs
CWE-183.question: Does this function check input against an allow list that admits entries, patterns or prefixes broad enough to let dangerous values through?

any: an allow list contains wildcards, broad patterns or prefixes such as allowing any host ending in a domain string without a leading dot
allowed values are tested with substring or startsWith matches, so evil.example.com.attacker.net passes
the list of permitted characters, tags, schemes or commands includes ones that are dangerous in the destination context
input is compared exactly against a small fixed set of known-safe values
domain or path checks parse the value first and compare the full host or canonical path exactly
the list is a deny list, which is a different weakness

distinguish_from.CWE-185: the allow list is a regular expression whose anchoring or syntax is wrong
distinguish_from.CWE-187: the defect is comparing only a prefix or part of a string

CWE-185.name: Incorrect Regular Expression
CWE-185.question: Does this function use a regular expression for validation or matching that is written wrongly, so it accepts or rejects the wrong inputs?

any: a validation regex lacks start and end anchors, or uses search where a full match was intended
an unescaped dot or other metacharacter makes the pattern broader than intended, such as a domain written with a bare dot
alternation without grouping, such as ^a|b$, anchors only part of the pattern
multiline mode lets ^ and $ match at inner line breaks, so a second line bypasses the check
the pattern is fully anchored, metacharacters are escaped and a full-match function is used
the regex is used only for searching or highlighting text, with no security or correctness decision
validation is done with a parser rather than a regex

distinguish_from.CWE-186: the pattern is too strict and rejects valid input
distinguish_from.CWE-1333: the pattern is correct but can backtrack catastrophically on crafted input

CWE-186.name: Overly Restrictive Regular Expression
CWE-186.question: Does this function use a regular expression that is too narrow, so harmful variants it was meant to catch slip past it?

any: a pattern meant to detect dangerous input matches only one spelling, such as lower case <script> without a case-insensitive flag
a deny pattern omits encoded, whitespace or alternative forms of the same token
a regex filter expects a fixed number of characters or a specific order that attackers can vary
input is canonicalised, for example decoded and lower-cased, before a broad pattern is applied
the regex is an anchored allow pattern, where narrowness only rejects input
the regex is not used for security filtering

distinguish_from.CWE-185: the pattern is too broad or wrongly anchored, so it accepts bad input

CWE-187.name: Partial String Comparison
CWE-187.question: Does this function compare only part of a string or buffer, such as the first n characters, when the whole value should match?

any: the length passed to a comparison comes from the shorter or the user-supplied string instead of the expected value
a credential, token or name is checked with startsWith or a prefix match
the comparison stops at the first mismatch in a way that treats a shorter input as matching
c: strncmp or memcmp is called with strlen of the user input or a fixed small length rather than the full expected length
cpp: expected.compare(0, input.size(), input) == 0 or expected.starts_with(input), so a shorter input matches

any: the full values are compared, with lengths checked to be equal first
the prefix comparison is intentional, such as routing on a path prefix, and has no security effect
c: strcmp is used, or strncmp with the length of the expected constant plus a check that the input ends there
cpp: the full std::string values are compared with operator==

distinguish_from.CWE-183: a whole-value allow list admits entries that are too broad

CWE-478.name: Missing Default Case in Multiple Condition Expression
CWE-478.question: Does this function branch on a value with a switch, match or if/else-if chain that has no default or final else for values it does not list?

any: a switch or multi-way branch over a state, command or enum value lists some cases and has no default branch
an if/else-if chain over the same variable ends without a final else, and later code assumes a variable set in one of the branches
python: a match statement has no case _ arm, or an if/elif chain over a mode or type leaves a result variable unset for other values

any: a default case or final else handles, rejects or reports unexpected values
the listed cases cover every possible value and the code after the branch does not depend on one of them running
typescript: the switch is over a union or enum and ends with an exhaustiveness check such as assigning to never

distinguish_from.REL-128: the construct is specifically a C or C++ switch with no default label
distinguish_from.REL-124: the construct is specifically a C or C++ else-if chain without a closing else

CWE-595.name: Comparison of Object References Instead of Object Contents
CWE-595.question: Does this function compare two objects, arrays or strings by reference or identity when it means to compare their contents?

any: two distinct objects or arrays are compared with == or ===, which is only true when they are the same object
c: two char pointers are compared with == or != instead of strcmp
struct or buffer contents are compared by comparing their addresses
cpp: pointers to objects or C strings are compared instead of the objects or std::string values
python: is or is not is used to compare strings, numbers, tuples or other values instead of ==

any: identity comparison is intended, such as checking for the same instance, a sentinel object or null
python: is None, is True or comparison with a module-level sentinel
rust: == on String, Vec or structs, which compares contents through PartialEq
cpp: == on std::string or types with an operator== that compares contents

distinguish_from.CWE-597: the operands are specifically strings compared with the wrong operator

CWE-597.name: Use of Wrong Operator in String Comparison
CWE-597.question: Does this function compare strings with an operator that tests identity or address rather than the characters?

c: char pointers or string literals are compared with == or != rather than strcmp or strncmp
cpp: two c_str() or data() results, or a const char* and a string literal, are compared with == so addresses are compared
python: strings are compared with is or is not, which depends on interning
javascript: String objects created with new String are compared with == or ===, or a string is compared with a wrapper object
rust: string data is compared by pointer, for example with as_ptr or std::ptr::eq, instead of ==

any: strings are compared with the language's content comparison, such as strcmp, std::string ==, Python == or JavaScript === on primitive strings
c: a pointer is compared with NULL or with another pointer to check whether they refer to the same buffer

distinguish_from.CWE-187: the string comparison is by content but covers only part of the string

CWE-697.name: Incorrect Comparison
CWE-697.question: Does this function compare values, strings, patterns or floating-point numbers in a way that could give the wrong answer?

any: string, list or regular expression checks used for validation, filtering or access decisions
comparisons of objects, references, mixed types or partial strings, or switch and if chains deciding on a value
floating-point equality, tolerance, NaN-sensitive comparisons, sorting or min/max over floats, or floats as map keys
range checks with only an upper or only a lower bound
the function performs no comparisons beyond simple loop counters against a fixed length
the function only moves, formats or stores data with no decision logic

CWE-839.name: Numeric Range Comparison Without Minimum Check
CWE-839.question: Does this function check that a signed number is below a maximum but never that it is at or above the minimum before using it?

c: a signed int index, length or offset is tested only with value < max or value <= max and then used to index, allocate or copy
a size from input is stored in a signed type and only an upper limit is checked, so a negative value passes
the lower bound check is present on some paths but missing on another path that reaches the use
cpp: a signed index is checked only as i < static_cast<int>(v.size()) or i < max, then used with operator[] or begin() + i

c: both bounds are checked, for example value >= 0 && value < max
the value has an unsigned type, or is converted to unsigned before a single upper-bound test
the value is a constant or comes from a source that cannot be negative, such as sizeof or strlen
cpp: the index is std::size_t, or a >= 0 test precedes the comparison with size()

distinguish_from.CWE-129: the value is an array index whose validation is missing entirely or wrong in another way

CWE-1023.name: Incomplete Comparison with Missing Factors
CWE-1023.question: Does this function decide something by comparing values while leaving out a factor that the decision needs, such as the full length, a lower bound or a case?

any: a comparison considers only part of the relevant data, for example a prefix, one field of a composite key or the first n bytes
a range check tests only the upper bound of a signed value, or only the lower bound
a switch or if chain handles some values and has no branch for the rest
typescript: an if chain or switch over a union, enum or discriminant covers only some members, with no default and no never exhaustiveness check

any: every field and the full length are compared, and both range bounds are tested
every possible value is handled, including a default or final else
typescript: the final branch assigns the value to a variable of type never or calls an assertNever helper, so the compiler reports any missed member

distinguish_from.CWE-187: the missing factor is the remainder of a string
distinguish_from.CWE-478: the missing factor is a default or final else branch
distinguish_from.CWE-839: the missing factor is a minimum bound on a numeric range

CWE-1024.name: Comparison of Incompatible Types
CWE-1024.question: Does this function compare values of different types, so the comparison converts one of them or can never be true?

any: a value of one type is compared with a value of an unrelated type, such as a number with a string, or an enum with a raw integer
c: a signed value is compared with an unsigned one, such as int with size_t, so a negative value converts to a large positive number
a pointer is compared with an integer, or char with a value outside its range such as EOF stored in a char
cpp: a signed int that may be negative is compared with size(), std::string::npos or another unsigned size_type value
javascript: loose == or != between different types, such as a string from input against a number or a boolean
typescript: an operand typed any, or one produced by an as cast, is compared with == or === against a number, string or boolean of another type
python: a str read from input is compared with == to an int, or bytes with str, so the test is always false

any: both operands are converted explicitly to the same type with validation before comparison
cpp: the comparison uses std::cmp_less, std::ssize or operands that are both the container's size_type
javascript: strict === or !== is used and both sides have the same type
typescript: both operands have declared non-any types and the comparison compiles, as the compiler rejects comparisons between types with no overlap
rust: ordinary comparisons, which the compiler rejects across different types unless cast explicitly

distinguish_from.CWE-597: the operands are strings compared by reference rather than content

CWE-1025.name: Comparison Using Wrong Factors
CWE-1025.question: Does this function compare the wrong things, such as the wrong variable, field, size or a value with itself, so the check does not test what it means to?

any: a variable is compared with itself, or with a different but similarly named variable from the one just computed
a check compares an identity, reference or handle when it needs the contents, or the contents when it needs identity
a length is compared with a capacity in different units, such as characters against bytes
c: sizeof a pointer is used where the size of the pointed-to buffer was meant
cpp: sizeof is applied to a std::string, std::vector or std::span object where its size() was meant
smart pointers, iterators or c_str() pointers are compared with == where the pointed-to contents were meant

any: the operands are the values the surrounding logic computes and uses, in the same units
the comparison is a deliberate idiom, such as x != x to detect NaN, with a comment or obvious intent

distinguish_from.CWE-595: object references are compared where their contents were intended
distinguish_from.REL-191: the wrong factor is a fixed absolute tolerance for floating-point equality

CWE-1077.name: Floating Point Comparison with Incorrect Operator
CWE-1077.question: Does this function compare floating-point values with an operator that ignores rounding, precision differences or NaN?

any: computed floating-point results are compared with == or !=
a float of one precision is compared with an expression in another precision
a floating-point loop counter or accumulator is tested for exact equality with a target value
comparison uses a suitable relative tolerance or a library closeness function
the compared values are exact, such as integers stored in floats, zero from assignment, or a constant copied unchanged

distinguish_from.REL-190: exact equality is tested between computed floating-point values
distinguish_from.REL-204: a narrower float variable is compared with a wider expression
